claims.text: Romosozumab, a monoclonal antibody against sclerostin, has antiresorptive and anabolic effects; it raises hip and spine bone density and reduces fractures in postmenopausal women.
claims.quote: Romosozumab is a monoclonal antibody against sclerostin (a small protein made by osteocytes that inhibits new bone formation by osteoblasts). It has both antiresorptive and anabolic effects and has been shown to increase bone mineral density in the hip and lumbar spine and reduce fracture risk in postmenopausal women (26).

claims.text: For severe osteoporosis, especially older, frail patients and those at risk of falling, or a fracture despite adequate antiresorptive therapy; monthly subcutaneous injection for 1 year,
claims.quote: Romosozumab is indicated for patients with severe osteoporosis, particularly in older adults, those who are frail, and those with an increased risk of falling. It should also be considered in patients who fracture despite adequate antiresorptive therapy. It is given via monthly subcutaneous injection for 1 year (27).

claims.text: then an antiresorptive (eg, alendronate or denosumab) to prevent rapid bone loss.
claims.quote: Romosozumab treatment for 1 year followed by alendronate for 1 year is more efficacious than treatment with alendronate for 2 years (28), and romosozumab for 1 year followed by denosumab for 2 years decreases fracture risk and increases bone mineral density (28). As with denosumab, when romosozumab is discontinued, antiresorptive therapy should be given to prevent rapid bone loss (29).

claims.text: Boxed warning: increased MI, stroke and cardiovascular death; don't start within 12 months of an MI or stroke.
claims.quote: Romosozumab carries a boxed warning due to increased risk for cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction, stroke, and cardiovascular death. Romosozumab should not be initiated within 12 months of a patient having had a myocardial infarction or stroke.
